chapter.title: Writing a brief the builder can't misread

cards.body: Tell a builder "make the kitchen nicer" and you get back a kitchen, nicer in the one way they happened to like. Claude Code is the same: it fills every gap you leave with its own guess, and it guesses fast. **A good brief closes the gaps before the builder starts**: who it's for, the one job, what finished looks like, and what to leave alone.
cards.simpler: Tell a builder "make the kitchen nicer" and you get a kitchen that is nicer in the one way they liked. Claude Code works the same way. Any gap you leave, it fills with its own guess, and it guesses fast. **A good brief closes the gaps before the builder starts.** Say who it is for, the one job, what finished looks like, and what to leave alone.

cards.prompt: Your neighbour Dev wants a tip calculator. Which of these 3 requests gets him the closest first version from Claude Code?

options.text: "Make a tip calculator and make it nice."
"A one-page tip calculator for me, on my phone, at restaurants. I type the bill, tap 15%, 18% or 20%, and see the tip and total. No sign-in, no history."
"Build the best tip calculator you can. Surprise me."

whyNot.a: That's the "make it better" trap, not a brief: "nice" has no picture, so Claude paints its own.
whyNot.c: That's handing over the decisions, not just the hammer: "surprise me" means you spend the next hour un-surprising yourself.

cards.reteach: A brief works when someone else could check it. "Nice" can't be checked. "I type a bill, tap 18%, see the total" can: you either see it or you don't. Say who, the one job, what you'll see, and what to skip.

cards.title: Who, and the one job
cards.body:
Start with one person and one moment. *The user* is just whoever will tap the thing, even if it's you tonight on the couch. "For me, on my phone, at a restaurant" tells Claude the screen is small and the hands are busy.

Then the one job. A work order that says "kitchen and bathroom and maybe the roof" gets a builder who starts three things and finishes none. Pick one verb: track, calculate, list, remind. **One user, one job** is the whole first line of your brief.

You'd think more detail is what helps. It does, but only after these two are nailed down.
cards.simpler:
Start with one person and one moment. *The user* is whoever will tap the thing, even if that is you tonight on the couch. "For me, on my phone, at a restaurant" tells Claude the screen is small and your hands are busy.

Then pick one job. A work order that says "kitchen, bathroom, maybe the roof" gets a builder who starts three things and finishes none. Pick one verb: track, calculate, list, remind. **One user, one job** is the first line of your brief. More detail helps, but only after these two are set.

cards.title: Priya's plant app
cards.body: Priya has 11 houseplants and keeps killing the fern. Her first brief was "an app to help me with my plants". Claude built a plant encyclopedia with 400 species and a search bar. Her second brief: "For me, at home. One job: remind me which plants to water today. Done looks like a list of plant names with a Water button next to each; tap it and the plant drops off until its next day. No photos, no species database." The fern lived.
cards.simpler: Priya has 11 houseplants and keeps killing the fern. Her first brief was "an app to help me with my plants". Claude built a plant encyclopedia with 400 species and a search bar. Her second brief said: "For me, at home. One job: remind me which plants to water today. Done looks like a list of plant names with a Water button next to each. Tap it and the plant drops off until its next day. No photos, no species database." The fern lived.

cards.prompt: Marco wants a page to split a dinner bill. He writes: "For me and 3 friends after dinner. One job: split a bill evenly. Leave out: tips, uneven splits, saving past dinners." Which line is he missing?

options.text: What done looks like: "I type the total and the number of people, and see what each person owes."
The programming language Claude should use.

whyNot.a: That's decoration, not the brief: colours are a one-line fix later, and Claude picks fine defaults.
whyNot.c: That's the builder's choice of tools, not yours: you hired Claude so you don't have to pick the saw.

cards.reteach: The 4 lines are who, one job, what you'll see when it's done, and what to leave out. Marco has 3 of them. Without "done looks like", Claude has to guess whether the page shows a number, a table or a chart.

cards.title: Done, and the don'ts
cards.body:
*Done looks like* is a sentence you could check with your eyes: "I type 60, pick 4 people, see 15." Not "it works well." A builder shown a photo of the finished shelf builds that shelf. One without the photo builds a shelf.

The last line is the one people skip: what to leave out. Claude is generous. Ask for a list and you may get sorting, search, dark mode and an export button. "No sign-in, no saving, no settings" keeps the first version small enough to test in 2 minutes.

**Say what you'll see, and what you won't.** Short brief, fewer round trips.
cards.simpler:
*Done looks like* is a sentence you can check with your eyes. "I type 60, pick 4 people, see 15." Not "it works well." A builder shown a photo of the finished shelf builds that shelf. One without the photo builds some shelf.

The last line is the one people skip: what to leave out. Claude is generous. Ask for a list and you may also get sorting, search, dark mode and an export button. "No sign-in, no saving, no settings" keeps the first version small enough to test in 2 minutes. **Say what you'll see, and what you won't.**

cards.body: Sam types "make it better" after the first version. Claude changes the fonts, adds a settings page and renames two buttons. Sam liked the buttons. Spot it: if your request has no noun you could point at on the screen, it isn't a brief yet. "Make the total bigger and bold" is one.
cards.simpler: Sam types "make it better" after the first version. Claude changes the fonts, adds a settings page and renames two buttons. Sam liked the buttons. Here is how to spot the problem. If your request has no noun you could point at on the screen, it is not a brief yet. "Make the total bigger and bold" has one. **If you can't point at it, it isn't a brief yet.**

cards.prompt: A friend asks you to check their brief before they send it: "Build me something for my running. Make it clean and modern." What do you tell them?

options.text: Add the 4 lines: who, the one job, what done looks like, what to leave out.
Add more adjectives so Claude understands the vibe.
Send it as is; Claude will ask questions if it's confused.

whyNot.b: That's more paint on a blank work order: adjectives like "clean" give Claude a mood, not a picture to build.
whyNot.c: That's hoping the builder stops to ask; Claude usually guesses and builds, so you find the gap after, not before.

cards.reteach: A brief is 4 lines: who will use it, the one job, what you'll see on screen when it's done, and what to leave out. If you can't check a line by looking at the screen, it isn't a done-looks-like line yet.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A brief is 4 short lines: who uses it, the one job, what you'll see when it's done, and what to leave out. **If you can't check a line by looking at the screen, rewrite it.**

Tomorrow: a small web app is only 4 kinds of files. Which does what?
cards.simpler:
A brief is 4 short lines. Who uses it. The one job. What you will see on the screen when it is done. What to leave out. **If you can't check a line by looking at the screen, rewrite it.** Think of it as a photo of the finished shelf, not a wish for a nicer kitchen.

Tomorrow: a small web app is only 4 kinds of files. Which does what?

cards.body: Open Claude Code in your folder from chapter 1. Write a 4-line brief for the tiniest thing you want tonight: who, one job, done looks like, leave out. Send it. Count the round trips.
cards.simpler: Open Claude Code in your folder from chapter 1. Write a 4-line brief for the tiniest thing you want tonight. Who is it for. What is the one job. What does done look like on the screen. What should be left out. Send it. Then **count the round trips**, meaning how many times you had to go back and ask for changes before it matched what you pictured.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write a 4-line brief that gets Claude Code to a testable first version in 1 or 2 rounds.
